newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to cut 1997 deficit to 2.9% of GDP - papers.
newsitem.headline: France to cut 1997 deficit to 2.9% of GDP - papers.

text.p: France intends to cut its public deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, newspapers reported on Wednesday.
The central government deficit would be 283.6 billion francs in 1997, well above the government's target of less than 250 billion, financial and other dailies reported.

The papers reported that the government's 1997 budget, to be presented to the cabinet later on Wednesday, has held to its commitment of freezing central government spending at the 1996 level, which is expected to be 1,552.9 billion francs.
Daily Le Figaro said that debt charges for the government would rise from 226 billion francs in 1996 to 245 billion in 1997 and that civil service pay would climb by 1.7 percent.

It said that spending cuts will total more than 60 billion francs and that government spending would rise by 1.5 percent next year. The government's budget projects that receipts will rise by 2.0 percent next year, Le Figaro said.

The government is expected to announce a net cut of 5,600 civil servants. As expected, the government will cut 15 billion to 20 billion francs from employment subsidies and 13 billion francs from housing subsidies.
Financial daily Les Echos said the government would forecast a social security deficit next year of 35 billion francs.
The Social Security Accounts Commission would announce next week that the 1996 deficit was expected to total 49.5 billion francs, it said.
The government planned to raise five billion francs by increasing excise duties on alcohol and tobacco to help finance the welfare system.
Government officials refused to comment on the newspaper reports. The government was also due to announce how it planned to reduce the deficit to two percent of GDP in 2001.
